title: Home Hygiene & Sanitation Practices
subtitle: Block the routes germs use to reach your family, using clean hands, safe water, clean toilets, a hygienic kitchen and safe waste habits, and turn those skills into a paid service.
description: A practical course on keeping a Nigerian home clean and safe, built on WHO guidance. You will learn how diarrhoea, cholera and Lassa fever germs reach people, then set up handwashing, safe drinking water, toilet, kitchen, pest and waste routines that block each route. The course ends with first aid, knowing when to seek care, and pricing a cleaning or hygiene service.
outcomes: Map your home's germ risks on the F-diagram and choose the barrier for each one
Wash hands the WHO way and build a working jerrycan handwashing station
Treat and store drinking water safely and plan your household's daily water needs
Run cleaning, toilet, pest and waste routines that a whole household or compound can share
Recognise diarrhoea and its danger signs and give correct first aid for home injuries
Cost and price a home cleaning or hygiene service with a clear profit
audience: Women managing a household or compound, and anyone who wants to offer cleaning or hygiene services, with no previous training needed.
tools: A smartphone for photos, a stopwatch and notes
Soap, a 5-litre jerrycan or large bottle, and basins
Rubber gloves, cloths in two colours and household bleach
Containers with lids for water, food and waste
A notebook and pen for rotas, logs and costings

modules.title: Germs, Clean Hands and a Cleaning Routine
modules.overview: Start with how disease-causing germs travel from faeces to mouth in a normal home, and where you can block them. Then master the WHO handwashing method, build a simple handwashing station, and set up a cleaning schedule your household can actually keep.

lessons.title: The F-diagram: how germs travel from faeces to mouth, and where to block them
objectives: Explain in plain words how diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid germs reach a person's mouth
Draw the F-diagram and name its five routes: fluids, fingers, flies, fields and food
Match each route to a household barrier: toilet, handwashing, safe water or food hygiene
Use symptom timing to work out when and where an infection may have started

blocks.text: Most of the stomach illnesses that hit Nigerian homes, such as diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery and typhoid, are caused by germs that live in human faeces. A **germ** is a living thing too small to see, such as a bacterium, a virus or a parasite. One person may carry these germs without looking sick. WHO notes that most people infected with cholera bacteria have no symptoms, yet they can pass the bacteria in their faeces for 1 to 10 days. So a clean-looking person, a clean-looking cup or clear-looking water can still carry germs.

The germs only make someone ill when they get into the mouth and are swallowed. Health workers call this the **faecal-oral route**: from faeces to mouth. It sounds unpleasant, but understanding it is the most useful idea in this whole course, because every hygiene habit you will learn is simply a way of blocking that route.

blocks.name: microbe
blocks.caption: Germs are too small to see, so we follow their routes instead of trusting our eyes.

blocks.text: The five F routes
Water and sanitation workers use a simple picture called the **F-diagram**. It shows five paths that start with the letter F and carry germs from faeces to a new person.

head: Route
How germs travel in a real home
Example
rows: Fluids (water)
Faeces leak into a well, stream or broken pipe, or a dirty cup is dipped into stored drinking water
A family drinks from a shallow well near a pit latrine
Fingers
Hands touch faeces when using the toilet, cleaning a child's bottom or touching dirty surfaces, then touch food or mouth
Mama cleans the baby, then serves rice without washing
Flies
Flies land on open faeces or uncovered toilets, then on food
Fried fish left uncovered near an open drain
Fields (soil)
Open defecation or spilled faeces in the yard; children play there and put hands or toys in mouths
A toddler crawling behind the house where an older child squatted
Food
Food is contaminated by any of the routes above, or washed in dirty water, and eaten raw or poorly reheated
Salad vegetables rinsed in water from an unprotected source

blocks.title: From faeces to a new person
items: Faeces
Fluids, fingers, flies, fields
Food
Mouth of new person
blocks.caption: Germs leave faeces, travel by four routes, often reach food, and are swallowed by the next person.

blocks.text: Barriers: where you break the chain

A **barrier** is anything that stops germs moving along a route. The strongest barrier is the first one: keeping faeces safely inside a clean toilet or latrine, so germs never reach water, hands, flies or soil. This is called a **primary barrier**. The second line of defence, **secondary barriers**, stops germs that have already escaped: washing hands with soap, treating and storing water safely, covering and cooking food properly, and keeping flies away.

items: **Safe toilet use and cleaning** blocks all routes at the source (Module 3).
**Handwashing with soap** at key moments blocks the fingers route (Lesson 2).
**Safe water treatment and storage** blocks the fluids route (Module 2).
**Covered food, clean kitchen, fly control** block the flies and food routes (Module 2).
**Clean yard and safe disposal of child faeces** block the fields route (Module 3).

blocks.text: WHO lists the same set of protections for diarrhoeal disease: safe drinking water, improved sanitation, handwashing with soap, exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, and rotavirus vaccination. No single habit is enough on its own. A family that washes hands well but drinks contaminated water is still exposed, which is why this course covers every route.
Timing tells you where to look

Germs do not cause illness the moment they are swallowed. There is a waiting period, called the **incubation period**, before symptoms appear. For cholera, WHO says symptoms appear 12 hours to 5 days after infection. For Lassa fever, which you will meet in the pest control lesson, the incubation period is 2 to 21 days. Knowing this helps you think back sensibly: the meal just before the illness is not always the cause.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a run of diarrhoea in a shared compound
blocks.context: For example, Bisi lives in a compound in Ibadan with four households sharing one borehole tap and one toilet. On Thursday morning, three children from two different households have watery diarrhoea.
steps: Bisi notes the time symptoms began: Thursday, about 6 a.m. If this were cholera, infection could have happened 12 hours to 5 days earlier, so anywhere from Saturday morning to Wednesday evening.
She lists what the two affected households shared in that window: the borehole water, the toilet, and rice and stew bought from the same roadside seller on Tuesday.

She walks the F-diagram. Fluids: the tap is fine but one household fills drinking water into an open bucket and dips cups in it. Flies: the toilet door does not close and flies gather. Fingers: there is no soap near the toilet.
She does not try to prove the exact cause. Instead she closes the gaps on every route: a lidded water container with a tap, soap and water beside the toilet, and a repaired toilet door.
Because watery diarrhoea can be cholera, she makes sure the children start oral rehydration solution (ORS) and are taken to the nearest health centre.
blocks.result: The compound blocks three routes in one day for a small cost, and the sick children get care early instead of waiting to see who is to blame.

blocks.title: Diarrhoea is a warning sign, not a small matter
blocks.text: WHO warns that severe cholera can kill within hours if untreated. Watery diarrhoea in a child, or many cases at once in your area, needs ORS and a visit to a health facility. Do not give any medicine without a health worker's advice. Module 4 covers danger signs in detail.

Keep the F-diagram in your head as you move through this course. Each time you learn a new habit, ask: which route does this block? If you cannot answer, the habit may be for comfort or appearance rather than health. Both have value, but health comes first.

takeaways: Diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid germs travel from faeces to mouth.
The five routes are fluids, fingers, flies, fields and food.
A safe toilet is the primary barrier; handwashing, safe water and food hygiene are secondary barriers.
Healthy-looking people, clear water and clean-looking hands can still carry germs.
Symptoms appear after an incubation period, so look back days, not just hours.

activity.title: Map your home on the F-diagram
steps: Draw the F-diagram on a sheet of paper: faeces on the left, mouth on the right, five routes in between.
Walk round your home and compound and write one real risk you see beside each route.
Beside each risk, write the barrier that would block it.
Circle the two gaps you can fix this week for little or no money.
Fix one of them and note the date.
activity.evidence: A photo of your hand-drawn F-diagram with your home's risks and the barrier you fixed

lessons.title: Handwashing the WHO way, the key moments and a home handwashing station
objectives: Wash your hands using the WHO steps in 40 to 60 seconds
List the key moments when hands must be washed with soap
Build a low-cost handwashing station with a jerrycan, soap and a drain
Calculate how much water and soap your household's handwashing uses

blocks.text: Handwashing with soap is one of the protections WHO lists against diarrhoeal disease. It blocks the **fingers** route of the F-diagram. Water alone is not enough: soap lifts grease and dirt off the skin and the rubbing and rinsing carry germs away. The method matters too. Most people rinse only their palms and miss the fingertips, the thumbs and the backs of the hands, which are exactly the parts that touch food and faces.

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.alt: A person washing hands with soap at a sink
blocks.caption: Good handwashing covers every surface of both hands, not just the palms.

blocks.text: The WHO handwashing steps
WHO's How to Handwash guide says the whole procedure should take **40 to 60 seconds**. Here are the steps in plain words.

items: Wet your hands with clean water.
Apply enough soap to cover all surfaces of both hands.
Rub palm against palm.
Put your right palm over the back of your left hand with fingers interlaced and rub, then swap hands.
Rub palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
Rub the backs of your fingers against the opposite palm with fingers interlocked.
Clasp your left thumb in your right palm and rub in a circle, then swap.
Rub the clasped fingertips of your right hand in a circle in your left palm, backwards and forwards, then swap.
Rinse your hands with water.
Dry thoroughly with a single-use towel (or let them air dry; do not wipe on your wrapper or a shared damp cloth).
Use the towel to turn off the tap, so clean hands do not touch a dirty tap.

blocks.title: Count it out
blocks.text: Most people stop after about 10 seconds. To reach 40 seconds, count slowly to 40 while rubbing, or sing a short song twice. Children learn this quickly when an adult does it with them.
The key moments at home
Washing hands at the wrong time protects nobody. These are the moments that matter most in a household, because they are where hands meet faeces or food.

items: After using the toilet or latrine.
After cleaning a child's bottom, changing a nappy or handling child faeces.
Before preparing food and again after handling raw meat, fish or chicken.
Before eating, and before feeding a child.
After touching rubbish, animals or cleaning a toilet.
Before and after caring for someone who is sick.

blocks.title: Hands through the day
items: Toilet or child care
Wash with soap
Prepare food
Wash again
Eat or feed child
blocks.caption: Each time hands move from a dirty task to food or a mouth, a handwash breaks the chain.

blocks.text: A handwashing station that needs no plumbing

Many homes do not have a sink with running water. People then share one bowl of water, which simply spreads germs from hand to hand. A better choice is a station where clean water flows over the hands and away. You can make one from a jerrycan or a large plastic bottle.

items: Take a clean 5-litre jerrycan or bottle with a cap. Make a small hole near the bottom on one side, or fit a cheap plastic tap if you can buy one.
Hang or place it at a height where both adults and children can reach, next to the toilet and near the kitchen if possible.
Hang a bar of soap in an old onion net or stocking tied to the frame, so it stays clean and dry and does not get lost. Liquid soap in a small squeeze bottle also works.
Put a small bed of stones or gravel, or a basin you empty daily, under the stream so the waste water does not make a muddy pool where mosquitoes can breed.
Refill with clean water every day and wash the container each week.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much water and soap the station needs
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano has six people in her home and sets up a 5-litre jerrycan station beside the toilet. She wants to know how often to refill it.
steps: She fills the jerrycan with 5 litres and counts washes until it runs out: 20 washes. So one wash uses 5 / 20 = 0.25 litres.
She estimates each person washes at 5 key moments a day: 6 people x 5 = 30 washes a day.
Daily water: 30 x 0.25 = 7.5 litres. That is one and a half jerrycans, so she refills in the morning and again after lunch.
A bar of soap in a net lasts her household 10 days. In a 30-day month that is 30 / 10 = 3 bars.
blocks.result: Halima knows the station needs 7.5 litres of water a day and about 3 bars of soap a month, so she plans water fetching and buys soap in a pack of three.

blocks.title: When there is no soap and water
blocks.text: An alcohol-based hand rub is useful when hands are not visibly dirty, for example on a bus. When hands are visibly dirty or greasy, or after the toilet, soap and water is the right choice. Keep a spare bar of soap so the station is never left without one.

Finally, make handwashing easy to remember. Put the station in the path people already walk: between the toilet and the house, or at the kitchen door. A station hidden behind the house will be forgotten.

takeaways: WHO handwashing takes 40 to 60 seconds and covers palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and fingertips.
Wash after the toilet or child care, before food preparation, before eating and feeding a child.
Running water from a jerrycan beats a shared bowl.
Measure your station's water use so it never runs empty.
Place the station where people already walk.

activity.title: Build and test your handwashing station
steps: Set up a jerrycan or bottle station with soap in a net and a drain underneath.
Count how many washes one full container gives and calculate litres per wash.
Calculate daily water need for your household at 5 washes per person.
Teach one family member the WHO steps and time them with your phone.
Note any problems after three days and fix them.
activity.evidence: A photo of your working station and a note with your water calculation and the timed wash

lessons.title: Cleaning versus disinfecting, and a daily, weekly and monthly schedule
objectives: Explain the difference between cleaning and disinfecting, and when each is needed
Clean a room in the right order: top to bottom, cleanest to dirtiest
Use household bleach and other cleaners safely, following the label
Write a daily, weekly and monthly schedule and share tasks fairly

blocks.text: A home can look tidy and still carry germs on the places hands touch most. A cleaning routine is not about making the house look perfect. It is about removing dirt and germs from the right places, often enough, without wasting money or harming anyone with chemicals.

blocks.name: clean-up
blocks.alt: A person sweeping and tidying a room
blocks.caption: A routine works when it targets the places germs collect, not only what looks dirty.

blocks.text: Cleaning and disinfecting are different jobs

**Cleaning** means removing dirt, grease and many germs with water, soap or detergent and scrubbing. **Disinfecting** means using a chemical, such as household bleach, to kill germs that remain. Cleaning always comes first, because dirt protects germs and stops a disinfectant from working. Pouring bleach on a dirty floor wastes bleach.

blocks.title: Clean or disinfect?
items: Clean only
Clean, then disinfect
right: Surfaces touched by vomit or diarrhoea
blocks.caption: Disinfect where faeces, vomit or raw meat juices may have been; everywhere else, good cleaning is enough.

blocks.text: Clean in the right order

items: Open windows for fresh air and put on gloves if you will use bleach.
Pick up items and rubbish first, so you can reach surfaces.
Work top to bottom: shelves and high surfaces before tables, tables before the floor, so falling dust lands on areas not yet cleaned.
Work cleanest to dirtiest: the living room before the kitchen, the kitchen before the bathroom, the bathroom basin before the toilet.
Use separate cloths for the toilet area and the kitchen. A simple colour rule helps, for example a red cloth only for the toilet.
Rinse, wring and hang cloths and mops to dry in the sun. Wet cloths left in a heap grow germs and smell.

blocks.text: High-touch spots

Germs spread most through the things many hands touch: door handles, light switches, the toilet flush handle or water bucket handle, taps, the fridge handle, TV remotes, phones and children's toys. Wiping these every day with a soapy cloth takes about five minutes and matters more than mopping every corner.

blocks.title: Using bleach and cleaners safely
blocks.text: Read and follow the dilution on the bottle label, because strengths differ between brands. Never mix bleach with other cleaners, especially toilet acids or ammonia products, as this can release dangerous gas. Dilute bleach in cold water, use it in a ventilated room, wear gloves, and make fresh diluted solution each day. Keep every chemical in its original labelled container, out of children's reach, and never pour it into a drink bottle.
Daily, weekly and monthly

head: How often
Tasks
Why
rows: Daily
Wash dishes and dry them on a rack; wipe kitchen surfaces; sweep the kitchen and entrance; wipe high-touch spots; clean the toilet seat and bowl; empty the kitchen bin; refill the handwashing station
Food crumbs and faeces attract flies and cockroaches within hours
Weekly
Mop all floors; wash bedsheets and towels; clean the bathroom fully; scrub the water storage container; wash and sun-dry cloths and mops; clear the yard and gutter near the house
Removes build-up before it smells or breeds pests
Monthly
Clean behind and under furniture and cookers; wash curtains; check stored food for weevils; check roof and walls for leaks and holes; turn mattresses and air them in the sun
Finds hidden pests, damp and damage early

blocks.title: Worked example: a fair weekly rota for a family of four
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Enugu lives with her husband and two children aged 9 and 13. She was doing all the weekly cleaning alone on Saturdays and it took most of the day.
steps: She times each weekly task once: mopping 40 minutes, bathroom 30 minutes, bedsheets and towels 60 minutes, water container 15 minutes, cloths and mops 15 minutes, yard and gutter 40 minutes.
Total weekly time: 40 + 30 + 60 + 15 + 15 + 40 = 200 minutes.
Shared by four people, that is 200 / 4 = 50 minutes each.

She assigns by age and safety: the 9-year-old does cloths and mops (15) plus part of the yard (35) = 50 minutes; the 13-year-old does mopping (40) plus the water container (15) = 55 minutes; her husband does sheets and towels (60); she does the bathroom with bleach (30) and the rest of the yard (5) and checks everything (15) = 50 minutes.
She writes the rota on paper and sticks it on the kitchen wall, with a tick box for each task.
blocks.result: Weekly cleaning drops from most of Saturday to one hour or less for each person, and the bleach task stays with an adult.

blocks.text: Review the schedule after a month. If a task is always skipped, it is either too long, placed on a bad day or given to the wrong person. Adjust it rather than giving up on the whole routine.

Cleaning tools need cleaning too. A mop left wet in a bucket, a broom full of hair and food, or a sponge used for a month will spread more dirt than it removes. Wash mop heads and cloths after use, shake out and rinse brooms weekly, replace sponges when they smell or fall apart, and store everything off the floor in a dry, airy place. Keep toilet tools in the toilet area only.

takeaways: Clean first to remove dirt; disinfect only where faeces, vomit or raw meat juices may have been.
Clean top to bottom and cleanest to dirtiest, with separate cloths for the toilet.
Never mix bleach with other cleaners; follow the label dilution and ventilate.
High-touch spots need a daily wipe.
Time your tasks, total them and share them fairly by age and safety.

activity.title: Write your household cleaning schedule
steps: List every daily, weekly and monthly task in your home.
Time each weekly task once with your phone stopwatch.
Add the minutes and divide fairly among household members, keeping chemical tasks with adults.
Write the rota with tick boxes and post it where everyone sees it.
After two weeks, note which tasks were missed and adjust.
activity.evidence: A photo of your posted rota with two weeks of ticks and your timing sums

quiz.q: Kemi's family drinks from a covered borehole, but her toddler often plays in the backyard where an older child sometimes defecates. Which F-diagram route is the main risk?
options: None, because the water is safe
quiz.explain: Faeces on the ground contaminate soil (fields), and a toddler's hands and toys carry germs to the mouth. Safe water does not block this route.

quiz.q: According to WHO, how long should a full handwash with soap and water take?
quiz.explain: WHO's How to Handwash guide gives 40 to 60 seconds for the whole procedure, enough time to cover every surface.

quiz.q: A jerrycan station gives 16 washes from 4 litres. A household of 5 washes at 5 moments each per day. How much water is needed daily?
quiz.explain: One wash uses 4 / 16 = 0.25 litres. Washes per day: 5 x 5 = 25. Water: 25 x 0.25 = 6.25 litres.

quiz.q: Ada wants to disinfect the toilet seat. What should she do first?
options: Clean off visible dirt with soapy water, then apply bleach diluted as the label says
Mix bleach with toilet acid for extra strength
Wipe it with the kitchen cloth
quiz.explain: Dirt protects germs, so cleaning comes first. Bleach is diluted as the label directs and never mixed with acids or other cleaners.

quiz.q: Which order of cleaning is correct for one day's housework?
options: Living room, then kitchen, then bathroom, finishing with the toilet
Toilet, then kitchen, then living room
Any order, as long as bleach is used
quiz.explain: Work from cleanest to dirtiest so germs from the toilet are not carried into the kitchen or living areas.

quiz.q: Three children fell ill with watery diarrhoea on Friday morning. If the cause were cholera, when could infection have happened?
options: Between about 12 hours and 5 days before Friday morning
It cannot be cholera if adults are well
quiz.explain: WHO gives cholera's onset as 12 hours to 5 days after infection, so the window runs back several days. Many infected adults have no symptoms.

modules.title: Kitchen, Water and Pest Control
modules.overview: The kitchen is where germs from hands, water, flies and rodents can end up in food. This module sets up a hygienic kitchen workflow, shows you how to make and keep drinking water safe at home, and how to keep rats, cockroaches, flies and mosquitoes out, including the steps WHO recommends against Lassa fever.

lessons.title: A hygienic kitchen: zones, cloths, chopping boards and the three-basin wash
objectives: Arrange your kitchen into raw, cooked and washing zones
Wash dishes with the three-basin method and dry them off the floor
Manage kitchen cloths, sponges and chopping boards so they do not spread germs
Apply WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food when storing cooked food and leftovers

blocks.text: Most kitchen illness does not come from dramatic mistakes. It comes from small, repeated habits: the same wet cloth used on the table, the plates and the baby's face; raw chicken cut on the board that later holds sliced tomatoes; dishes washed in one basin of grey water and stacked on the floor. This lesson fixes those habits one by one, using what you already have.

blocks.name: woman-cooking
blocks.alt: A woman cooking at a stove
blocks.caption: A hygienic kitchen is mostly about workflow: where things go and in what order.

blocks.text: Three zones, even in a small kitchen

Even a corner kitchen or an outdoor cooking area can have three zones. A **raw zone** for cutting raw meat, fish, chicken and unwashed produce. A **cooked and ready zone** for serving food, slicing bread and preparing salads. A **washing zone** for dishes, with dirty items arriving from one side and clean items leaving on the other. Keep raw and ready foods apart, and never carry a dripping bag of raw meat across the ready zone.

blocks.title: One-way kitchen flow
items: Raw food in
Raw zone: wash, cut
Cook thoroughly
Ready zone: serve
Washing zone
blocks.caption: Food moves one way, from raw to cooked to served, so germs from raw food never reach ready food.

blocks.text: Chopping boards and knives

Use two boards if you can: one for raw meat, fish and chicken, and one for ready foods, vegetables you will eat raw, and bread. Mark them, for example with a notch or a coloured handle. If you have only one board, cut ready foods first, then raw meat, then wash the board and knife with hot soapy water before using them again. Replace boards with deep cuts, because germs hide in the grooves.
Cloths and sponges

A damp kitchen cloth that stays warm and wet all day is one of the dirtiest things in a home. Give cloths separate jobs: one for dishes, one for wiping surfaces, one for drying hands, and never use a kitchen cloth on the floor or the toilet. Wash cloths in hot soapy water at the end of each day and hang them in the sun to dry fully. Rotate so that a fresh, dry cloth is ready each morning.
The three-basin dish wash

items: Scrape food scraps into the bin, not into the wash water.
Basin 1, wash: warm water with dishwashing liquid. Wash glasses and cups first, then plates, then pots, so the water gets dirty last with the greasiest items.
Basin 2, rinse: clean water to remove soap and loosened dirt. Change it as soon as it looks cloudy.
Basin 3, optional sanitising rinse for boards and items that touched raw meat: clean water with a disinfectant made up exactly as its label directs.
Dry: place items upside down on a raised rack or clean tray, never on the floor. Air drying is cleaner than wiping with a used cloth.
Empty the basins away from the house and food area, rinse them and store them upside down.

blocks.title: The one-basin habit
blocks.text: Washing every plate in a single basin of water means the last plate is rinsed in the dirtiest water of the day. A second rinse basin is the cheapest hygiene upgrade in most homes.
Storing food and leftovers

WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food are: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. In Nigerian homes where stew is kept for several days, bring it back to the boil each time rather than just warming it, keep the pot covered and use a clean spoon for serving. Do not leave cooked food standing out for hours in a hot kitchen; eat it, or cover it and store it cool. Cover all food against flies. Store dry foods in sealed containers off the floor, which also keeps rats out, as you will see in Lesson 3.

blocks.title: Worked example: upgrading a kitchen in one weekend
blocks.context: For example, Amina runs a busy household of seven in Kaduna. She uses one basin for dishes, one cloth for everything and stacks clean plates on a mat on the floor. She has about 15,000 naira (approximate) to spend.
steps: She buys a second plastic basin (about 2,500 naira, approximate) for rinsing.
She buys a dish rack (about 6,000 naira, approximate) so plates dry off the floor.
She buys a pack of six cloths in two colours (about 3,000 naira, approximate): three blue for dishes and drying, three yellow for surfaces.
She buys a second small chopping board (about 2,500 naira, approximate) and marks the raw one with a red ribbon on the handle.
She uses the remaining 1,000 naira towards dishwashing liquid and writes the new kitchen rules on a card by the sink.
blocks.result: For about 14,000 naira (approximate) Amina has a rinse basin, a drying rack, colour-coded cloths and separate boards, which closes several germ routes she used every day.

blocks.text: Prices change by city and month, so treat these figures as a guide. The principle stays the same: spend first on the habits that touch food most often.

takeaways: Keep raw, ready and washing zones, and move food one way.
Use separate boards for raw meat and ready food, or wash between uses.
Give cloths separate jobs and dry them fully in the sun every day.
Wash dishes in one basin, rinse in a second, and dry them off the floor.
Follow WHO's Five Keys: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, use safe water.

activity.title: Kitchen hygiene upgrade
steps: Sketch your kitchen and mark the raw, ready and washing zones.
Set up the two- or three-basin dish wash and a raised drying place.
Label or colour-code your cloths and chopping boards.
Use the new system for one week and note what was hard to keep up.
Write a short list of costs if you bought anything.
activity.evidence: A before and after photo of your washing area and your zone sketch

lessons.title: Safe drinking water: choosing a source, treating it at home and storing it safely
objectives: Explain why clear water can still be unsafe and which diseases it can carry
Treat water at home by settling, filtering and bringing it to a rolling boil
Store treated water so it is not re-contaminated
Plan how much water to treat and store for your household each day

blocks.text: WHO explains that drinking water contaminated with germs can transmit diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio. Water from a well, borehole, stream, tanker or roadside seller may look clear and still contain germs from faeces. Even water that leaves a borehole clean often becomes dirty at home, through a dirty bucket, an open drum or a cup dipped in with unwashed hands. Safe water needs three things: a good source, treatment where needed, and safe storage.

blocks.name: potable-water-symbol
blocks.alt: A symbol of a tap with drinking water
blocks.caption: Safe drinking water means a protected source, treatment when needed and clean, covered storage.

blocks.text: What a safe source looks like

WHO describes a **safely managed** drinking water service as an improved source located on the premises, available when needed and free from contamination. Improved sources include piped water, boreholes, protected wells and protected springs. An unprotected well, a stream or pond, or water from a cart or tanker you cannot check, should always be treated before drinking. A well or borehole near a latrine, soakaway or rubbish heap can also be contaminated, so check what lies uphill of it.
Treating water at home

items: Settle: if water is cloudy, let it stand in a covered container for several hours so dirt sinks to the bottom, then pour off the clearer water without stirring the bottom.
Filter: pour the settled water through a clean cloth folded several times, or a household water filter, to remove more particles. Cloth filtering alone does not make water safe.

Disinfect by boiling: bring the water to a **rolling boil**, where big bubbles rise strongly and keep coming even when you stir. WHO states that heating water to a rolling boil is enough to inactivate disease-causing bacteria, viruses and protozoa.
Or disinfect with a household treatment product such as chlorine tablets or liquid, using exactly the amount and waiting time on its label. Do not guess the dose.
Cool the boiled water in the same covered pot, then pour it into a clean storage container.

blocks.title: Boiling safely
blocks.text: Boil water on a stable stove with the pot handle turned inward, away from children. Never leave a pot of boiling water where a child can pull it. Burns from hot water are common in homes; the first aid lesson in Module 4 covers what to do.
Storing water so it stays safe

blocks.title: Safe water storage check
items: Container has a lid
Narrow mouth or a tap
Raised off the floor
Cleaned every week
No dipping with hands or cups
blocks.caption: Treated water stays safe only when hands and dirty cups cannot get into it.

blocks.text: The best container has a narrow opening and a tap at the bottom, so people pour water out instead of dipping into it. If you only have a wide bucket, keep a clean long-handled ladle hanging on a hook beside it and use it only for that water. Wash the container every week with soap and clean water, rinse it well, and let it dry. Keep drinking water separate from water for washing and cleaning, and label which is which. A covered container also stops mosquitoes from breeding in your water.

head: Common habit
Risk
Better practice
rows: Dipping a cup into the drum
Hands and cup carry germs into all the water
Use a container with a tap, or a dedicated ladle
Open drum in the yard
Dust, leaves, animals and mosquitoes get in
Keep a tight lid on, and raise the drum off the ground
Topping up old water with new
Old contamination and sludge stay forever
Empty, wash and dry the container before refilling
Same jerrycan for kerosene and water
Chemical poisoning
Mark one container for water only; never reuse chemical containers

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a day's safe water
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Onitsha has a family of five. They buy water from a tanker and she is not sure of its source, so she decides to boil all drinking water. She has a 4-litre pot and two 10-litre containers with taps.
steps: She measures for three days how much drinking water her family uses, including water for the baby's cup and for mixing drinks: about 11 to 12 litres a day. She plans for 12 litres.
Number of boils: 12 / 4 = 3 pots a day. She boils one pot in the morning and two in the evening, when the stove is already on for dinner.
Storage: two containers hold 2 x 10 = 20 litres. She uses one container while the other is being filled and cooled, then swaps.
Every Saturday she washes and sun-dries each container in turn as it empties, before refilling it, so both are cleaned weekly.
She labels the containers DRINKING WATER in marker and keeps them on a raised table with a cover.
blocks.result: Ngozi produces 12 litres of boiled water a day with three boils, always has one full container ready, and nobody dips cups into the drinking water.

blocks.text: If you buy sachet or bottled water, check the seal and the NAFDAC registration number printed on the pack, and store it out of direct sun. Wash your hands before opening a sachet with your teeth or fingers, since your mouth touches the outside of the sachet.

takeaways: Clear water can still carry cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea germs.
Settle and filter cloudy water first, then disinfect by rolling boil or a treatment product used as labelled.
Store treated water covered, raised, in a narrow-mouthed or tapped container.
Never dip cups or hands into stored drinking water.
Measure your daily need and plan boils and containers around it.

activity.title: Your household water plan
steps: Write down where your drinking water comes from and what lies near the source.
Measure how many litres of drinking water your household uses for three days.
Choose your treatment method and calculate how many batches you need a day.
Set up a covered, raised, labelled storage container with a tap or ladle.
Add container washing to your weekly cleaning rota.
activity.evidence: A written one-page water plan with your calculations and a photo of your storage container

lessons.title: Keeping rats, cockroaches, flies and mosquitoes out, and protecting against Lassa fever
objectives: Explain how rats, flies, cockroaches and mosquitoes put a household at risk
Apply WHO's household steps against Lassa fever: rodent-proof food storage and clean surroundings
Clean up rodent droppings safely
Carry out a pest-proofing audit of your home and cost the repairs

blocks.text: Pests are not only a nuisance. Flies carry germs from faeces to food, as you saw in the F-diagram. Cockroaches walk through drains and rubbish and then across plates. Mosquitoes breed in standing water and spread malaria. And in Nigeria, rats are linked to **Lassa fever**, a serious viral illness. The good news is that the same few habits control all of them: take away their food, water and shelter, and close the ways in.

blocks.name: rat
blocks.caption: Rats come for food and shelter; take both away and they move on.

blocks.text: Lassa fever and rats

WHO explains that the main animal source of Lassa virus is the **Mastomys** rat, commonly called the multimammate rat, which lives in and around homes. People are infected mainly through contact with food or household items contaminated with rat urine or faeces. The incubation period is 2 to 21 days. WHO's household advice is to store grain and food in **rodent-proof containers**, keep the household clean and dispose of rubbish far from the home, and cook food thoroughly. When caring for a sick person, family members should avoid contact with blood and body fluids.

items: Never dry grain, garri, rice or pepper on the bare ground or on the roadside where rats run at night; dry on a raised mat and bring it in before dark.
Store all grain and dry foods in containers with tight lids: plastic buckets, metal tins or drums, not open sacks or baskets.
Cover cooked food and wash pots the same night; do not leave food in pots on the floor overnight.
Keep rubbish in a bin with a lid, and take it far from the house as often as possible.
Close gaps under doors, holes in walls and open drain pipes with cement, wood or wire mesh.

blocks.title: Cleaning rat droppings and nests
blocks.text: Do not sweep droppings dry, as this raises dust. Wear gloves, wet the droppings and the area first with soapy water or a disinfectant made up as its label directs, wait a few minutes, then wipe up with paper or a cloth you throw away in a tied bag. Wash gloved hands, remove the gloves, then wash your hands with soap. Throw away any food that rats have touched.
Cockroaches, flies and mosquitoes

head: Pest
What attracts it
What to do
rows: Cockroaches
Food crumbs, grease, dirty dishes left overnight, damp sinks and drains
Wash dishes the same day, wipe grease, dry the sink area at night, seal cracks, keep drain covers on
Flies
Uncovered food, open rubbish, faeces in uncovered toilets or the yard, animal dung
Cover food, keep bins closed, keep the toilet lid or cover on, clean animal areas daily
Mosquitoes
Standing water in buckets, tyres, cans, blocked gutters and plant pots
Cover water containers, empty and scrub anything holding water each week, clear gutters and drains, sleep under a treated net
Rats and mice
Food in sacks, rubbish, clutter and holes
Rodent-proof containers, clean yard, sealed holes, rubbish far from the home

blocks.title: Pest control, most to least effective
items: Remove food and water
Close entry points
Clean and declutter
Traps
Poisons, used last and carefully
blocks.caption: Prevention at the base does most of the work; chemicals are a last step, not the first.

blocks.title: Rat poisons and insecticides
blocks.text: Many rat poisons and insecticides are dangerous to children, pets and food. Use only registered products, follow the label exactly, place baits where children and animals cannot reach, keep them away from food and water, and store them locked in their original containers. Never decant poison into a food or drink container. Wear gloves to pick up a dead rat and put it in a tied bag for disposal far from the home.

blocks.title: Worked example: a pest-proofing audit and budget
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Ondo hears rats in the ceiling at night and finds droppings in her storeroom. Her family keeps garri, rice and beans in open sacks.
steps: She walks round the house with a notebook and finds 3 holes at the base of the walls, a kitchen drain with no cover, and a gap of about 2 cm under the back door.
Food storage: she needs containers for garri, rice and beans. She buys 3 plastic buckets with tight lids at about 3,500 naira each (approximate): 3 x 3,500 = 10,500 naira.

Repairs: a small bag of cement to fill the wall holes, about 6,000 naira (approximate); a piece of wire mesh for the drain, about 1,500 naira (approximate); a rubber door sweep, about 2,500 naira (approximate).
She cleans the storeroom safely using the wet method, throws away a sack of rice with droppings in it, and moves the rubbish heap to the collection point further from the house.
blocks.result: For about 20,500 naira (approximate) Funke removes the rats' food supply and entry points, which follows WHO's household advice against Lassa fever.

blocks.text: Check again after two weeks. Fresh droppings mean an entry point is still open. Look for droppings and greasy rub marks along walls to find the route, and seal what you find.

takeaways: WHO links Lassa fever to Mastomys rats and food or items contaminated with their urine or faeces.
Store grain and food in rodent-proof containers and dispose of rubbish far from home.
Wet droppings with soapy water or disinfectant before wiping; never sweep them dry.
Remove food, water and entry points first; use poisons last and lock them away.
Empty or cover anything holding water each week to stop mosquitoes breeding.

activity.title: Pest-proofing audit
steps: Walk round your home and list every hole, gap, open drain and uncovered food or water container.
Mark signs of pests: droppings, gnawed sacks, cockroaches at night, mosquito larvae in water.
Make a repair and container list with approximate prices and a total.
Fix the cheapest high-risk items this week.
Re-check after two weeks and record any new signs.
activity.evidence: Your audit list with costs and before and after photos of one repair or food store

quiz.q: Rukayat has one chopping board. She needs to slice tomatoes for salad and cut raw chicken. What is the safest order?
options: Chicken first, then tomatoes, then wash
Either order, as long as she rinses with cold water
Cut both at the same time to save time
Tomatoes first, then chicken, then wash board and knife with hot soapy water
quiz.explain: Cut ready-to-eat food first so raw chicken juices never reach it, then wash the board and knife properly before any further use.

quiz.q: What does WHO say about heating water to a rolling boil?
options: It is enough to inactivate disease-causing bacteria, viruses and protozoa
It only works if boiled for an hour
quiz.explain: WHO states a rolling boil is sufficient to inactivate pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa. It does not remove chemicals or cloudiness, which is why settling and filtering come first.

quiz.q: A family needs 15 litres of boiled drinking water a day and has a 5-litre pot. How many boils a day?
quiz.explain: 15 / 5 = 3 boils a day.

quiz.q: Ifeoma finds rat droppings on her kitchen shelf. What should she do?
options: Sweep them quickly onto the floor and out of the door
Blow them away with a fan
Wear gloves, wet them with soapy water or disinfectant, then wipe up and bag the waste
Leave them; they dry out and become harmless
quiz.explain: Dry sweeping raises dust. Wetting first and wiping with gloves, then bagging the waste and washing hands, follows safe practice against Lassa fever.

quiz.q: Which storage is safest for treated drinking water?
options: An open bucket with a cup inside
An old kerosene jerrycan, rinsed out
A basin covered with a cloth on the floor
A covered container with a tap, raised off the floor
quiz.explain: A tap and lid stop hands and cups contaminating the water, and raising it keeps dirt and animals away. Chemical containers must never be reused for water.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food?
options: Wash fruit in the same water as dishes
Store food on the floor to keep it cool
Use one cloth for all kitchen jobs
quiz.explain: The Five Keys are keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials.

modules.title: Toilets, Children and Waste
modules.overview: The toilet is the primary barrier against faecal germs, so this module starts with keeping toilets and latrines clean, covered and working, including shared compound toilets. It then turns to teaching children hygiene habits that last, and finishes with sorting, storing and disposing of household waste safely.

lessons.title: Clean, safe toilets and latrines, including the shared compound toilet
objectives: Explain why a clean, working toilet is the primary barrier against faecal germs
Clean a flush toilet and a pit latrine in the right order with the right tools
Spot warning signs of a full pit or failing septic tank and act early
Organise a fair cleaning and supplies rota for a shared toilet

blocks.text: WHO lists diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera and dysentery, typhoid, intestinal worms, polio, schistosomiasis and trachoma among the diseases spread by poor sanitation. A toilet protects a family only when faeces stay inside it: when the bowl or slab is clean, the hole is covered, flies cannot get in and out, and nothing leaks into drains or wells. A dirty toilet also pushes people, especially children, to go outside, which brings germs back into the yard.

blocks.name: toilet
blocks.caption: A clean, covered, working toilet keeps faeces away from water, hands, flies and soil.

blocks.text: Types of household toilets

head: Type
Where the waste goes
Main hygiene points
rows: Flush or pour-flush toilet
Into a septic tank and soakaway, or a sewer
Keep enough water for flushing; clean the bowl, seat and handle; only toilet paper and water down the drain
Pit latrine with slab
Into a pit below a concrete or plastic slab
Keep the slab dry and clean; keep the drop hole covered with a lid; keep the door and walls in repair
Ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine
Into a pit with a vent pipe and fly screen on top
Keep the screen intact and the inside dim so flies are drawn to the light at the vent, not the door

blocks.text: Cleaning the toilet, step by step

items: Put on rubber gloves and use the toilet-only cloth and brush. Keep these tools in the toilet area, never in the kitchen.
Open the window or door for air.

Clean from cleanest to dirtiest: door handle and light switch, then the flush handle or water bucket handle, then the seat top and lid, then the bowl outside, then under the seat, and the bowl inside last.
Scrub the inside of the bowl with a toilet brush and detergent. For a pit latrine, scrub the slab and footrests with soapy water and sweep water away from the hole, not into it if your pit is small.
Disinfect the seat, handle and slab with bleach diluted as its label says. Never mix bleach with toilet acid or other cleaners.
Rinse the brush, stand it to dry, wash gloves with soap, take them off, then wash your hands with soap.

blocks.title: Daily toilet check
items: Hole or lid covered
Seat and slab clean, dry
Water or flush working
Soap at handwashing point
Bin with lid for pads
blocks.caption: Five quick checks each day keep the toilet working as a barrier.

blocks.title: What not to put in a toilet or pit
blocks.text: Sanitary pads, nappies, plastic, rags and bottles block pipes, fill pits quickly and make emptying harder. Wrap used pads and disposable nappies in paper or a bag and put them in a covered bin. Do not pour large amounts of bleach or chemicals into a pit latrine or septic tank.
When the pit or septic tank needs attention

WHO warns that poorly designed and managed pits and septic tanks contaminate open drains and groundwater. Warning signs include a bad smell that does not go away after cleaning, slow flushing, waste rising close to the slab, wet patches or bad-smelling water near the soakaway, and many flies. Do not wait for an overflow. Arrange emptying by a proper desludging service that takes the waste to an approved site, and ask your local government environmental health office which services operate in your area. Never let anyone empty a pit by hand into a nearby gutter or open land.
Making a shared toilet work

In many compounds several households share one toilet. Problems usually come from unclear responsibility rather than bad people. A written rota, shared supplies and a simple daily check make a big difference.

blocks.title: Worked example: a rota for a toilet shared by six households
blocks.context: For example, the six households in Ruth's compound in Port Harcourt share one pour-flush toilet. It is often dirty and the soap always runs out. Ruth proposes a plan at a compound meeting.
steps: Cleaning: each household takes one day a week, Monday to Saturday. On Sunday the households take turns, so each covers one Sunday every six weeks.
Supplies per month: detergent about 2,500 naira, bleach about 2,000 naira, soap about 1,500 naira, gloves and a brush replacement about 1,800 naira (all approximate).
Total supplies: 2,500 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 1,800 = 7,800 naira a month.
Each household pays 7,800 / 6 = 1,300 naira a month into a small kitty kept by one person, who records payments and purchases in a notebook.
A checklist with the five daily checks is pinned inside the door, and the day's household ticks it before 8 p.m.
blocks.result: For about 1,300 naira (approximate) per household a month, the compound has a clean toilet, constant soap and a clear record of who did what.

blocks.text: Agree a fair rule for elderly or disabled neighbours, for example another household covering their day in exchange for something else they can contribute. A rota everyone feels is fair is the one that lasts.

takeaways: A clean, covered, working toilet is the primary barrier against faecal germs.
Clean from the door handle to the inside of the bowl, with toilet-only tools.
Wrap pads and nappies and bin them; do not put them in the toilet or pit.
Act early on a filling pit or failing septic tank and use a proper desludging service.
A written rota and a shared supplies kitty keep a shared toilet clean.

activity.title: Toilet audit and plan
steps: Use the five daily checks to inspect your toilet or latrine and note what fails.
Clean it fully using the step-by-step order.
List the supplies you need each month with approximate prices and a total.
If the toilet is shared, draft a rota and a cost share per household.
Pin the checklist inside the toilet door.
activity.evidence: Photo of the clean toilet, the pinned checklist and your supplies cost sheet

lessons.title: Teaching children hygiene habits that stick, from potty to school age
objectives: Handle and dispose of child faeces and nappies safely
Teach a child handwashing using demonstration, practice and praise
Set up a child-height handwashing point and a daily routine
Track a child's progress with a simple chart and calculate the success rate

blocks.text: Young children are the family members most at risk from diarrhoeal disease. WHO describes diarrhoea as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months. Children put hands and objects in their mouths, crawl on floors and play in soil, so they meet the fingers and fields routes every day. They also learn by copying. A child who sees adults wash hands every time learns the habit far faster than one who is only told.

blocks.name: children
blocks.caption: Children learn hygiene by watching and copying adults every day.

blocks.text: Child faeces are not harmless
Many families believe a baby's faeces are clean. They are not: they carry the same germs as adult faeces, and often more. Treat them with the same care.

items: Put a baby's or toddler's faeces into the toilet or latrine, never into the yard, a drain or the general rubbish.
Empty a potty into the toilet, rinse it, clean it with soapy water, and wash your hands with soap afterwards.
For cloth nappies, tip solid faeces into the toilet first, then soak and wash nappies separately from other clothes and dry them in the sun.
For disposable nappies, tip solids into the toilet where possible, roll the nappy up, wrap it and put it in a covered bin.
Wash your hands with soap after every nappy change, and wash the child's hands too if they touched the area.

blocks.text: Teaching handwashing: show, do, praise

items: Show: wash your own hands slowly next to the child, saying each step aloud: wet, soap, palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, rinse, dry.
Do together: guide the child's hands through each step. Use a short song or counting game so they keep rubbing long enough.
Let them try alone while you watch, and correct gently.
Praise the effort straight away and specifically: 'You washed your thumbs, well done.'
Repeat at the same moments every day: after the toilet, before eating and after playing outside, so it becomes automatic.

blocks.title: Hygiene skills by age
items: Baby: adults wash baby's hands
Toddler: copies with help
Ages 4 to 5: washes with reminders
School age: washes alone, teaches siblings
blocks.caption: Expect more independence as the child grows, but keep checking and praising.

blocks.text: Common mistakes when teaching children

head: Mistake
What happens
Better approach
rows: Washing for the child every time, even at school age
The child never learns to do it alone
Hand over one step at a time and step back as each is mastered
Rinsing without soap because soap 'wastes'
Germs stay on the hands
Hang soap in a net so it lasts, and use a small amount each wash
Sharing one bowl of water among several children
The last child washes in everyone's germs
Pour water over hands from a jug or use a tippy-tap
Telling the child off for forgetting
Hygiene becomes a source of fear and hiding
Give a calm reminder and praise the next correct wash

blocks.text: Older children can become your best helpers. A 9- or 10-year-old who has mastered the steps can lead younger siblings at mealtimes, which reinforces the habit for both of them. Praise the older child for teaching, not only for washing.
Make it easy for small hands

Set up a handwashing point the child can reach without help: a low stool by the sink, or a small tippy-tap or bottle station at child height near the toilet. Hang soap in a net so it does not slip away. Keep a separate small towel for each child, or let hands air dry. Trim fingernails short every week, since germs collect under long nails, and bathe children daily, especially after play in soil or dust.

blocks.title: A school hygiene pouch
blocks.text: Give a school child a small pouch with a piece of soap in a container and a clean handkerchief, and a bottle of safe water from home. Show them how to use it before eating at school.

blocks.title: Worked example: a two-week handwashing chart
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos wants her 5-year-old son Tunde to wash his hands at 5 moments a day: after the toilet (counted once a day), before breakfast, before lunch, before dinner and after playing outside.
steps: She draws a chart with 14 rows (days) and 5 columns (moments). Possible ticks: 14 x 5 = 70.
In week 1, Tunde washes properly 22 times out of 35. Success rate: 22 / 35 x 100 = about 63%.
She notices he forgets most after playing outside, so she moves his stool and soap to the back door where he comes in.
In week 2 he scores 31 out of 35. Success rate: 31 / 35 x 100 = about 89%.
Over the two weeks: 22 + 31 = 53 out of 70, which is about 76%.
blocks.result: Tunde's handwashing rose from about 63% to about 89% in one week after Grace moved the washing point to where the habit was being missed.

blocks.text: Use stickers or a star for each tick if the child enjoys it, but avoid punishment. The goal is a habit the child owns, not a fear of being caught.

takeaways: Child faeces carry dangerous germs; put them in the toilet and wash hands after.
Teach handwashing by showing, doing together, letting them try and praising specifically.
Put a handwashing point at child height where the habit is needed.
Trim nails weekly and bathe children daily.
A simple chart shows progress and where the routine breaks down.

activity.title: Child hygiene routine
steps: Set up a child-height handwashing point with soap in a net.
Teach a child in your home the handwashing steps using show, do, praise.
Run a one-week tick chart for 5 moments a day.
Calculate the success rate and change one thing where the habit is missed.
Run a second week and compare.
activity.evidence: Photo of the child-height station and your two-week chart with percentages

lessons.title: Household waste: sorting, storing, composting and safe disposal
objectives: Sort household waste into food waste, recyclables and other waste
Store waste so it does not attract flies, rats or mosquitoes
Start a simple compost for food and garden waste
Estimate your weekly waste and plan collection or disposal

blocks.text: Rubbish around a home feeds the pests you met in Module 2. Food scraps attract rats and flies, old tins and tyres hold rainwater where mosquitoes breed, and blocked gutters flood homes in the rainy season. WHO's Lassa fever advice includes disposing of garbage far from the home. A simple sorting and storing system cuts the amount you throw away, keeps the compound clean and can even give you compost for a garden.

blocks.name: wastebasket
blocks.caption: A lidded bin, emptied often, keeps food waste away from flies and rats.

blocks.text: Sort at the source

head: Type
Examples
What to do
rows: Food and garden waste
Peels, leftover food, leaves, grass
Compost it, or keep it in a lidded bin and empty it daily
Recyclables
PET bottles, cans, cartons, clean paper and cardboard
Rinse, flatten, store dry in a bag; sell or give to collectors or recyclers
Other waste
Dirty plastic bags, wrappers, wrapped pads and nappies, broken items
Bag tightly and store in a lidded bin for collection
Hazardous items
Batteries, old medicines, chemical containers, broken glass, used razor blades
Keep apart, wrap sharp items in thick paper or a tin, and ask your health centre or waste service how to dispose of them

blocks.title: From kitchen to final disposal
items: Sort at source
Store in lidded bins
Compost or recycle
Collect or dispose away from home
blocks.caption: Sorting first makes the remaining rubbish smaller, cleaner and easier to handle.

blocks.text: Store it so pests cannot use it

items: Use bins with tight lids, raised off the ground if possible, and away from the kitchen door and water storage.
Line the bin with a bag and tie it before it overflows.
Wash bins weekly with soapy water and leave them to dry in the sun.
Never leave rubbish in a heap near the house, in drains or on the roadside. Drains blocked with rubbish cause flooding and hold standing water.
Turn over or throw away containers, tyres and tins that can collect rainwater.

blocks.title: Do not burn plastics
blocks.text: Burning rubbish, especially plastics and foam packs, releases harmful smoke that children and neighbours breathe. Use a collection service where one exists. If you must burn garden waste, keep it small, away from buildings, and never with plastics, aerosol cans or batteries.
Simple home composting

items: Choose a shaded spot away from the house and the water source, or use a large container with holes drilled in the bottom and a lid.
Add a layer of dry material (dry leaves, grass, shredded paper or cardboard), then a layer of food scraps.
Cover every addition of food scraps with dry material so it does not smell or attract flies.
Keep it as damp as a squeezed sponge, and turn it with a stick every week or two.
Do not add meat, fish, bones, oil, dairy or faeces; these attract rats and dogs and can carry germs.
When it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil, use it on your garden or pot plants.

blocks.title: Worked example: a week's waste and a collection plan
blocks.context: For example, Esther lives in Lagos with her family of five. Their rubbish heap behind the kitchen attracts flies and rats, and she wants to switch to the registered collection service for her street.
steps: For one week she sorts waste into three 20-litre buckets. At the end of the week she has filled food waste 4 times, recyclables 2 times and other waste 3 times.
Total volume: (4 + 2 + 3) x 20 = 180 litres a week.
Share of food waste: 4 / 9 x 100 = about 44%. If she composts it, the rubbish to collect falls to (2 + 3) x 20 = 100 litres.
Recyclables (40 litres a week) go to a collector who buys bottles and cans, so only 3 x 20 = 60 litres of other waste needs collection each week.
She checks with her street's registered waste collector (in Lagos these operate under LAWMA, the state waste agency) for the collection day and fee, and buys one lidded bin for the other waste.
blocks.result: By composting and recycling, Esther cuts the rubbish she needs collected from 180 litres to 60 litres a week, a reduction of two thirds, and clears the heap that drew rats.

blocks.text: Other states have their own waste agencies or local government arrangements. Ask at your local government environmental health office which collection service covers your area and what it costs, and do not pay cash to unregistered 'cart pushers' who dump waste in drains or on empty land.

Hygiene around waste also means protecting yourself. Wear gloves or use a tied bag over your hand when handling rubbish, never press waste down with bare hands, since broken glass and blades hide in bags, and wash your hands with soap after every bin trip. Teach children not to play in or near rubbish heaps or open drains.

takeaways: Sort waste into food, recyclable, other and hazardous at the source.
Use lidded, raised bins and wash them weekly; never heap rubbish near the house.
Do not burn plastics; use a registered collection service.
Compost food and garden waste, but not meat, oil, dairy or faeces.
Measuring your waste shows how much you can cut by composting and recycling.

activity.title: One-week waste audit
steps: Set up three containers: food waste, recyclables, other waste.
Count how many times you fill each in one week and calculate the litres.
Calculate the share of food waste and how much composting would cut.
Find out your area's waste collection service, day and fee.
Start a small compost or find a recycler for bottles and cans.
activity.evidence: Your tally sheet with calculations and a photo of your sorted bins or compost

quiz.q: Mariam's toddler has just used the potty. What should she do with the faeces?
options: Empty them into the toilet or latrine, clean the potty and wash her hands with soap
Throw them in the yard; child faeces are harmless
Put them in the kitchen bin
quiz.explain: Child faeces carry the same germs as adult faeces. They belong in the toilet, followed by cleaning the potty and handwashing.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order when cleaning a toilet?
options: Inside of the bowl first, then the door handle
Seat only, the rest does not matter
Door handle and flush handle, then seat, then bowl outside, with the inside of the bowl last
Pour bleach and toilet acid together, then rinse
quiz.explain: Clean from cleanest to dirtiest so the cloth does not carry germs from the bowl onto handles and the seat. Never mix bleach with acid cleaners.

quiz.q: Five households share a toilet and supplies cost 8,000 naira a month. How much does each pay?
quiz.explain: 8,000 / 5 = 1,600 naira per household per month.

quiz.q: A child washed hands correctly 28 times out of 35 chances in a week. What is the success rate?
Which item should NOT go into a home compost?
quiz.explain: Meat, fish, bones and oil attract rats and dogs and can carry germs, so they stay out of the compost.

quiz.q: Bola notices a strong smell that will not go away, slow flushing and wet, smelly ground near the soakaway. What should she do?
options: Pour a lot of bleach into the toilet daily
Have someone empty it by hand into the gutter
Arrange emptying by a proper desludging service and ask the local environmental health office
quiz.explain: These signs point to a full or failing septic system. WHO warns that poorly managed septic tanks contaminate drains and groundwater, so it needs proper emptying and safe disposal.

modules.title: Home Safety, Health Watch and Earning from Hygiene Skills
modules.overview: Hygiene work brings its own risks: cleaning chemicals, boiling water and sharp objects. This module covers storing chemicals safely and first aid for common home injuries, then how to watch for illness and know when to go to a health facility. It ends by turning your skills into a small, honest cleaning or hygiene service with correct pricing.

lessons.title: Safe storage of chemicals and first aid for burns, cuts and poisoning at home
objectives: Store bleach, kerosene, insecticides and medicines so children cannot reach or mistake them
Give correct first aid for a hot-water burn and a small cut
Respond correctly if a child swallows a chemical or gets it in the eye
Assemble and maintain a basic home first aid kit

blocks.text: The products that keep a home clean can also hurt the people in it. Bleach, toilet acid, kerosene, insecticide and rat poison are all dangerous if swallowed or splashed. Many child poisonings happen because a chemical was poured into a soft drink or water bottle and a child drank it. Boiling water for safe drinking, which you learned in Module 2, brings a burn risk. This lesson makes your hygiene routine safe as well as clean.

blocks.name: adhesive-bandage
blocks.caption: A small, stocked first aid kit lets you act correctly in the first minutes.

blocks.text: Store chemicals the safe way

items: Keep every chemical in its **original labelled container**. Never pour kerosene, bleach or insecticide into a drink bottle, water sachet or food tin.
Store chemicals high up or in a locked cupboard, out of children's sight and reach, and away from food and drinking water.
Keep caps tightly closed and buy containers with child-resistant caps where possible.
Store medicines separately from cleaning products, also out of reach, and never call medicine 'sweets' to a child.
Keep the product label readable, because it tells a health worker what was swallowed.
Never mix cleaning products, and never reuse a chemical container for water or food.

blocks.title: Chemical safety check
items: Original labelled container
High or locked away
Away from food and water
Caps tightly closed
Never mixed
blocks.caption: If any item fails, fix it today; most home poisonings start with one of these gaps.

blocks.text: First aid for common home injuries

head: Situation
Do
Do not
rows: Burn or scald from hot water or oil

Remove the person from the heat; cool the burn under cool, clean running water for a long time; remove rings or tight items near the burn before it swells; cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or cling film
Do not apply oil, palm oil, toothpaste, raw egg, butter or ice; do not burst blisters
Small cut or graze
Wash your hands; press with a clean cloth to stop bleeding; rinse the wound with clean water; cover with a clean dressing or plaster; change it if wet or dirty
Do not put ash, sand, herbs or powder in the wound
Chemical swallowed
Take the product away from the person; keep the container; go to the nearest health facility immediately with the container
Do not make the person vomit; do not give oil or palm oil 'to neutralise' it
Chemical in the eye
Rinse the eye straight away with plenty of clean running water, holding the eyelids open, and keep rinsing on the way to care
Do not rub the eye; do not put any other liquid in it

blocks.title: Go to a health facility straight away if
blocks.text: the burn is larger than the person's palm, is on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a joint, or is on a baby or young child; a cut will not stop bleeding with firm pressure or is deep or dirty; anyone has swallowed a chemical or medicine not meant for them; or a chemical has entered the eye. Ask the health worker whether a tetanus vaccine is due after a dirty wound. Do not give medicines without a health worker's advice.
Preventing burns while boiling water and cooking

items: Cook on a stable surface at standing height where possible, not on the floor where crawling children can reach.
Turn pot handles inward and keep hot drinks and kettles away from table edges.
Keep children out of the cooking area while you boil water or fry, for example with a low barrier or by giving older children the job of watching them elsewhere.
Let boiled water cool in the covered pot before pouring it into storage containers, and pour slowly with a dry cloth to hold the handle.

blocks.text: A basic home first aid kit

blocks.title: Worked example: building a first aid kit on a budget
blocks.context: For example, Uche in Owerri wants a basic kit in a clean plastic box with a lid, stored on a high shelf near the kitchen.
steps: Plastic box with a lid: about 1,500 naira (approximate).
Pack of plasters and two rolls of sterile gauze: about 2,500 naira (approximate).
A crepe bandage and a roll of plaster tape: about 2,000 naira (approximate).
Disposable gloves (a small pack) and a clean pair of scissors: about 2,500 naira (approximate).
A few sachets of oral rehydration salts (ORS) for diarrhoea, used as the pack or a health worker instructs: about 1,000 naira (approximate).
Total: 1,500 + 2,500 + 2,000 + 2,500 + 1,000 = 9,500 naira. She adds a card with the address and phone number of her nearest health facility.
blocks.result: For about 9,500 naira (approximate) Uche has a clean, labelled kit and a contact card, and she checks it every month to replace used or expired items.

blocks.text: Put first aid on your monthly cleaning checklist: open the box, replace what was used, check dates on ORS sachets, and make sure older children know where it is and when to call an adult.

takeaways: Keep chemicals in original labelled containers, high or locked away, never in drink bottles.
Cool burns with cool, clean running water; never apply oil, toothpaste or egg.
If a chemical is swallowed, do not make the person vomit; go to care with the container.
Rinse chemical splashes in the eye with plenty of clean running water and seek care.
Keep a stocked first aid kit and check it monthly.

activity.title: Home chemical and first aid check
steps: List every chemical in your home, where it is kept and in what container.
Move anything in a drink bottle or within a child's reach to a safe, labelled place.
Assemble or check your first aid kit and price any missing items.
Write your nearest health facility's address and number on a card in the kit.
Explain the burn first aid rule to one other adult in your home.
activity.evidence: Your chemical list showing fixes and a photo of your first aid kit with the contact card

lessons.title: Watching for illness: diarrhoea, dehydration, cholera and Lassa warning signs
objectives: Recognise diarrhoea using the WHO definition
Give the right home care: ORS, continued feeding and breastfeeding, with zinc only as a health worker advises
Identify danger signs that mean a person must go to a health facility now
Keep a simple family illness log to share with a health worker

blocks.text: Even a clean home cannot stop every illness. What matters next is spotting the illness early, giving the right care at home, and knowing exactly when home care is not enough. This lesson does not replace a health worker. It helps you act quickly and give the health worker clear information. Never give medicines, including antibiotics, without a health worker's advice.

blocks.name: medical-care
blocks.alt: A health worker caring for a patient
blocks.caption: Clear notes and early action help the health worker help your family.

blocks.text: What counts as diarrhoea

WHO defines diarrhoea as passing **3 or more loose or liquid stools a day**, or more often than is normal for that person. Frequent passing of formed stools is not diarrhoea, and breastfed babies often pass soft, pasty stools that are normal for them. The main danger of diarrhoea is losing water and salts from the body, called **dehydration**, which can become serious quickly in a small child.
Home care while you watch

items: Give **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**, mixed exactly as the sachet says with safe water. WHO notes that ORS costs very little and is the core treatment.
Keep feeding: continue nutritious food and keep breastfeeding during the illness, as WHO advises. Do not stop food to 'rest the stomach'.
Zinc supplements shorten an episode of diarrhoea in children, according to WHO; get them and the right amount from a health worker or pharmacist.
Keep up hygiene: wash hands after every nappy or toilet visit, put stools in the toilet, and disinfect surfaces soiled with diarrhoea or vomit.
Keep the sick person's cup, towel and plate separate while ill.

blocks.title: Diarrhoea: what to do
items: 3+ loose stools a day
Start ORS and keep feeding
Check danger signs
Any sign: go now
None: watch and record
blocks.caption: Start home care at once, but check for danger signs every few hours.

blocks.text: Danger signs: go to a health facility now

head: Sign
Why it matters
rows: Blood in the stool
WHO advises seeing a health worker when there is blood in stool
Diarrhoea that goes on for many days
WHO advises professional care for persistent diarrhoea
Signs of dehydration: very thirsty or unable to drink, sunken eyes, very sleepy or hard to wake, little or no urine, skin that goes back slowly when pinched
The body is losing more water than it is taking in
Large amounts of watery diarrhoea, especially with vomiting, or several people ill at once
This can be cholera, which WHO warns can kill within hours if untreated
Fever after contact with rats or a sick person, especially with bleeding, or fever that does not improve
Lassa fever and other serious infections need early testing and care

blocks.title: Cholera and Lassa: tell the health worker
blocks.text: If you suspect cholera or Lassa fever, tell the health worker what you have seen, such as many cases in the compound or rats in the house. These diseases are reported to public health authorities, and in Nigeria the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) coordinates outbreak response. When caring for a sick person, avoid contact with their blood and body fluids, as WHO advises, and wash your hands with soap after every contact.

blocks.title: Worked example: using an illness log to decide
blocks.context: For example, Fatima in Sokoto notices that her 2-year-old daughter has loose stools on Monday. She keeps a log in her phone notes.
steps: Monday: 7 a.m., 11 a.m., 3 p.m. and 8 p.m. loose stools. That is 4 in a day, so by the WHO definition it is diarrhoea. She starts ORS mixed with boiled water and keeps breastfeeding.
She checks danger signs at each change: the child drinks eagerly, passes urine, is playful between stools. No blood.
Tuesday: 3 loose stools, still drinking and playing. She continues ORS and food, and keeps hand hygiene strict.
Wednesday 10 a.m.: she sees blood in the stool. This is a danger sign, so she goes to the primary health centre that morning with her log.
The health worker reads the log: 4 stools Monday, 3 Tuesday, blood on Wednesday, ORS taken, still feeding. She examines the child and decides the treatment.
blocks.result: Fatima gave correct home care, recognised a danger sign the moment it appeared, and gave the health worker a clear three-day record instead of guesses.

blocks.text: Use the same log for fever, cough or vomiting: date, time, what you saw, what you gave and how the person is. Short notes are enough. Bring the log and any medicine packets to every visit.

Prevention and watching go together. When someone in the home is ill with diarrhoea or vomiting, step up the routines from earlier modules: clean and disinfect the toilet and any soiled surfaces daily, wash the sick person's bedding and clothes separately, keep them away from preparing food for others until they are well, and make sure every family member washes hands with soap after helping them. This stops one case becoming several.

takeaways: Diarrhoea is 3 or more loose or liquid stools a day, or more than normal for that person.
Start ORS at once and keep feeding and breastfeeding; zinc only as a health worker advises.
Blood in the stool, long-lasting diarrhoea, dehydration signs or heavy watery diarrhoea mean go now.
Tell the health worker about rats, other cases or contacts; avoid a sick person's body fluids.
A simple time-stamped log helps the health worker decide quickly.

activity.title: Family health watch kit
steps: Write the WHO diarrhoea definition and the danger signs on a card.
Set up an illness log template in a notebook or phone notes: date, time, signs, care given.
Check that you have ORS sachets and know how to mix them from the pack instructions.
Find and save the address and phone number of your nearest primary health centre.
Share the card with another carer in your home.
activity.evidence: Photo of your danger signs card and your blank log template

lessons.title: Turning hygiene skills into income: a home cleaning and sanitation service
objectives: Choose a hygiene service that fits your skills and local demand
Cost a cleaning job from supplies, transport, labour and equipment wear
Set a price with a clear profit and check it with a monthly projection
Run the service safely and honestly, with a checklist and a written quote

blocks.text: Everything you have learned in this course is a skill people pay for. Busy families, landlords, small offices, schools, clinics and event organisers need cleaning done properly and safely. Many cleaners work by habit; you can offer a service based on correct methods, with a checklist the customer can see. This lesson shows how to choose a service, cost it accurately and price it so you earn a real profit.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: A clear costing turns your hygiene skills into a service that pays.

blocks.text: Choose your service

head: Service
Who buys it
What you need
rows: Deep home cleaning
Working families, people moving house, before and after events
Cleaning tools, gloves, detergent, bleach, a helper, transport
Regular weekly cleaning
Busy households, elderly people living alone
Reliable schedule, basic tools, trust and references
Shared toilet and compound cleaning contract
Landlords and compound associations
Toilet-only tools, a rota checklist, monthly invoice
Household hygiene sessions
Women's groups, churches, mosques, schools
Your knowledge from this course, a handwashing station to demonstrate, clear handouts

blocks.title: From enquiry to repeat customer
items: Visit and assess
Written quote
Clean to checklist
Customer walk-through
Book next visit
blocks.caption: Assessing before quoting and checking with the customer after builds trust and repeat work.
